articles.title: Meta wants to pay for its broad AI buildout with a newly created class of stock
articles.author: Lucas Ropek
articles.content:
Meta is making a big push into AI, and it’s creating a new kind of stock that could help pay for it.

On Wednesday, as the company reported its third-quarter earnings, Semaforreportedthe company might issue non-voting stock, meaning shares that don’t give their owners a vote on company decisions, to help fund its push into artificial intelligence.

During Meta’s earnings call, the company confirmed that reporting. Meta’s chief financial officer, Susan Li, said the company plans to “create a new class of non-voting capital stock, which will be distributed to all existing shareholders through a stock dividend.”

Li later added that the company “created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, and other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.”

The shares will allow the company to maintain its current “founder-led structure,” she added. They will also expand its “funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business, driven by AI.”

Meta’s earnings were strong this past quarter, beating Wall Street expectations. The company made $64 billion in revenue, a jump of 26% from a year earlier. Its costs and expenses also rose too, however, by 68% year over year.

Reality Labs, the division responsible for Meta’s AR glasses, VR headsets, and VR software, continues to lose money, though less than it used to. The company said in its earnings report that it expects the division’s losses to shrink from its 2025 levels to between $18 billion and $19 billion.

Meta has made a big push into AI over the past year. The company has released several AI models, including Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer earlier this year. In recent weeks, it addedMuse Wonderand Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model whose underlying parameters are publicly available for outsiders to use and build on. Meta also launcheda coding agentfor software developers called Muse Code. At its Meta Connect event this year, the company announced a new line of cute and cuddly avatars for AI assistant, Meta Muse, in a push to make its AI services more relatable (and alsomeme-able).

As far as can be discerned, those AI products are doing well. “In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada have set up Muse personal agents,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s earnings call. “Growth continues to be strong, and we have been number one in the App Store almost every day.”

“Now that Muse has clear product-market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it,” Zuckerberg added, claiming later that the company expects to grow the product’s appeal to eventually “serve billions of people.”

The company also noted that certain storm clouds linger on the horizon in the form of ongoing regulatory and legal issues. “We continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” said Li. “For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets, and have a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the United States.”

articles.title: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI
articles.author: Aditya Mehta
articles.content:
Recursive, an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name. The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model,Flint, on Wednesday. Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI.

Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months.

Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI. It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry. Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control. For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop.

The company emerged from stealth in May with$650 million in fundingat a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist.

Because Flint runs on a user’s own computer rather than a company’s cloud servers, developers can use it offline, keep their code private, and avoid theusage feesthat AI cloud services charge based on how much text the model processes. The model is free to download on Hugging Face, the popular site for sharing AI models, under the Apache 2.0 license, an open source license that allows free use and modification.

Flint is a mixture-of-experts model, meaning it uses only a small slice of itself for any given task: just 2.5 billion of its 40 billion settings, known as parameters, at a time. That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’sMuse Spark Open, an open model built for Macs that was released last week. Muse Spark Open uses 816 billion parameters and needs at least a terabyte of memory.

Flint is also fast. In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. On Nvidia’s RTX Spark, Flint topped 150 tokens per second.

On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters. On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint.

The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps. Still, early reviews were positive. Wired’s Will KnightusedFlint on a Mac with 48GB of memory to build several small programs, including a to-do list app and a tool that scours the web for research. He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time.

The Eureka Machine comes up with ideas, runs experiments, and uses the results to decide what to try next. According to the company’slaunch video, it contributed to nearly every part of building Flint, from pretraining to post-training and inference.

Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations.

Recursive didn’t say how much time the Eureka Machine saved its researchers, but it’s not alone in leaning on AI to do research. OpenAI saidlast monththat by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher.

If Recursive’s bet pays off, each new model should be able to take on longer stretches of work without human help. The company previouslytold TechCrunchthat its $410 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services in June was “less about headcount and more about agent count.”

The longer-term goal, Socher told Wired, is for the Eureka Machine to achieve full recursive self-improvement, with humans overseeing the process and able to stop it if something goes wrong. Recursive says each new model should make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, helping it build the next one faster.

articles.title: Airbnb limits chores for guests, sparking backlash from hosts
articles.author: Lauren Forristal
articles.content:
Airbnb is taking steps to limit the chores that hosts can require of guests prior to checkout, addressing a long-standing grievance among customers who often pay cleaning fees and are told they must do a list of tasks themselves.

In a newpolicy update, Airbnb prohibits hosts from mandating that guests strip beds, wash and put away dishes, start laundry, or remove trash from the property. This new guideline will apply to reservations made on or after November 20.

This change comes in response to years of backlash regarding overly burdensome checkout instructions and hefty fines for not disposing of trash. Many guests have voiced their frustrations on social media, questioning why they should be responsible for cleaning tasks after already paying a cleaning fee.

However, some hosts aren’t pleased with the update. Within Airbnb’scommunity forums, some argue that basic cleaning responsibilities are essential for maintaining sanitary conditions and protecting their properties. They point out that hosts must manage the costs and practical demands of preparing their properties for the next guests.

One host expressed concern that the new policy leans toward a hotel-like model, which detracts from the unique appeal of Airbnb.

“Guests are given complete freedom to be lazy while the hosts bear the risk,” the host wrote. “The major distinction between commercial hotels and my private home is the personal touch. Guests can certainly be expected to wash their dishes or put them in the dishwasher and remove their dirty linens. In exchange, they enjoy a personal connection and a unique environment that a hotel simply can’t provide. Plus, every potential guest has the opportunity to read the listing beforehand and decide what they prefer. If these restrictions are removed, it could lead me to withdraw my listing and bid farewell to Airbnb after twelve years.”

Airbnb has outlined some exceptions to the new policy, though. Hosts may still ask guests to conserve water during droughts or use bear-proof trash containers in areas where wildlife poses a risk.

The policy change highlights the challenge Airbnb faces in balancing the expectations of guests versus hosts and is another step taken in addressing guests’ concerns. The company faced scrutiny in 2024 over price transparency from hosts tacking oncleaning feesafter guests booked their listings. In 2023, the company said more than 260,000 hosts had reduced or eliminated their cleaning fees. In May 2025, Airbnb begandisplaying total prices— including fees but excluding taxes — by default in search results worldwide.

It will be interesting to see how many hosts decide the new restrictions make Airbnb less attractive as a platform. But the move could also draw in more travelers who want the convenience of a rental without feeling as though they are both paying for housecleaning while still expected to clean the home themselves.

articles.title: Tesla starts Optimus robot production in California as profit falls 43%
articles.author: Kirsten KorosecSean O'Kane1:33 PM PDT · October 21, 2026
articles.content:
Tesla has started production of its Optimus humanoid robot at its factory in Fremont, California, in a manufacturing space once dedicated to making electric vehicles, the company announced Wednesday.

“The bots coming off this line are the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured,” Tesla wrote in itsthird-quarter letterto shareholders. “While we will continue to iterate on the hardware and manufacturing process, we have proven that the current manufacturing process for Optimus is suitable for a commercial product.”

Tesla CEO Elon Musk said on a conference call that he considers this “early production” and that the ramp will be slow and “somewhat bumpy because it is such a radically new product.” He nonetheless claimed Tesla will be able to make 20,000 of them per week by the end of 2027.

“There’s still some things we need to tweak about the design, because you need to deliver a robot that is safe and reliable and has long duration, so it can’t, like, wear out after a month,” he said. “And there’s still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks.”

That forward-looking development wasn’t enough to lift the company’s otherwise middling third-quarter earnings, results that typify a company in the midst of a major bet. Tesla’s revenue was flat and its expenses skyrocketed as it pressed the accelerator on its Optimus robots, AI, and autonomous driving. The end result was a 43% drop in profits.

The company’s revenue was largely driven by EV sales, which were flat year-over-year at $20 billion. Tesla delivered486,532 vehiclesin the third quarter, about 6,000 more than the previous quarter, but fewer than in the same period last year.

Tesla’s total third-quarter revenue was $28.04 billion, a skosh below the $28.09 billion it generated in the third quarter of 2025. Tesla’s third-quarter revenue was also about $200 million lower than the previous quarter’s haul of $28.23 billion.

Tesla saw a 16% year-over-year decline in revenue from its solar and energy storage business to $2.8 billion, which it blamed on tariff-related customer refunds. There was some positive revenue growth in its services business, a category that includes customer subscriptions to its Full Self-Driving advanced driver-assistance software. Tesla’s services business grew 33% year-over-year, bringing in $4.6 billion and accounting for a record $734 million in gross profit for the quarter.

None of this was enough to outpace Tesla’s spending on artificial intelligence projects and its Optimus robot, which took a big bite out of profits.

The company reported $787 million in net income, a 43% drop from the same period in 2025, when it earned $1.37 billion. Lower regulatory credit sales also put pressure on its profitability.

Tesla executives on the earnings call, including Musk, CFO Vaibhav Taneja, and Ashok Elluswamy, vice president of AI software at Tesla, all took bullish positions on the company’s FSD product, even as the timeline to give consumers the “unsupervised” version was delayed yet again. Today, Tesla owners can subscribe to a supervised version of the software that requires the driver to pay attention and be ready to take over at any time. The unsupervised version would be the equivalent of Level 4 autonomous driving capabilities similar to those used in robotaxis.

“We suspect somewhere around Q2 next year is when we can turn on some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the robotaxi fleet,” Elluswamy said, referring to when privately owned Tesla vehicles equipped with FSD (Supervised) would receive a software update enabling unsupervised driving.

Musk said during the company’s earnings call in April that the unsupervised version would “probably” be released in the fourth quarter of this year.

This story has been updated with information from Tesla’s quarterly conference call.

articles.title: Meta says Muse has over 10M users, with shopping a top activity
articles.author: Sarah Perez
articles.content:
Meta said during its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday that its AI app Muse has been adopted by more than 10 million users, confirmingestimates released earlier this weekby market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

But it is how people are using it and how much they’re spending that has caught CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s attention. Zuckerberg said about 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily, helping improve retention.

He also shared that over a quarter of Muse’s engaged users who were shopping via the AI agent had an average purchase size of over $200, which was surprising even to industry insiders.

“Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to the financial technology company that connects payment apps to customers’ bank accounts. Muse uses Plaid’s connector to enable agentic shopping.

Beyond shopping, Zuckerberg said other popular uses for Muse include personal productivity tasks, such as connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars. The exec stressed that this indicates users trusted Muse’s security setup, which includes a feature called “Muse Secure VM” designed to protect their data and privacy. He also mentioned that the forthcoming “Muse Confidential VM” will prevent even Meta from seeing users’ content.

Now that Muse has achieved “product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta’s focus will shift to scaling the AI agent, increasing revenue, and optimizing its compute costs. Remarkably, the tech company is forecasting that Muse will eventually bring in more revenue per user than its “family of apps” users do today — meaning its users on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. Currently, that figure is around “several hundreds of dollars annually,” Zuckerberg said.

Meta has said it ultimately intends to monetize Muse by keeping it free for most users but keeping a percentage of the commerce taking place on the platform. Power users who want access to the most advanced AI models or more tokens will also have to pay.

Zuckerberg also noted that Meta believes Muse will be profitable after it scales.

“On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years,” he told bankers and analysts on the Q3 earnings call. “In the near term, Muse is very compute-intensive to run, but we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale.”

Muse will also play a central role in Meta’s smart glasses strategy. Reality Labs, the division responsible for smart glasses, VR, and the metaverse, is still losing billions. However, thedivision’s lossesare expected to improve from $19.1 billion in 2025 to $15 billion this year.

Beyond scaling and supporting its hardware strategy, Zuckerberg teased the company’s plans for something he called the “Muse network.” He described this as taking Muse from a “single-player game” to one where “your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses].”

“And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” he added.

articles.title: The internet is having a very bad cybersecurity day
articles.author: Sarah Perez
articles.content:
The internet is having a bad day, from a cybersecurity perspective. Government websites around the worldwent offline, Reuters reported, after AI discoveredcritical security vulnerabilitiesthat impacted theprogramming language PHP. The issues were severe enough that theU.S. National Security Agency (NSA) advisedorganizations using PHP on their systems to either immediately update or take their systems offline until they could.

But the PHP update wasn’t the only headache cybersecurity folks were facing on Wednesday.Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment, also dropped a security surprise of its own when itsharedthat four high-severityvulnerabilitieswere just patched in its latest release. One allowed remote code execution, and two others would have permitted a TLS validation bypass, potentially allowing attackers to bypass checks intended to verify a server’s identity.

In addition, LiteLLM, a popular open source proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, wascompromisedby an attacker who injected malicious code, the company sharedin a post on Xon Wednesday afternoon. The malicious artifacts were published toPyPI(Python Package Index),Docker Hub, and GHCR (GitHub Container Registry), the post noted.

The malicious code was said to include an information stealer that targeted cloud credentials, passwords, and AI service credentials, in addition to a remote access trojan that could allow hackers to execute commands on compromised systems.

LiteLLM said it has now removed the malicious releases and images and advised anyone who installed them to followthe remediation guidanceit provided.

And wait, there’s more! An Indian certificate authority, eMudhra,had its private keys compromised, potentially allowing attackers to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites.Security pros have called thisa massive cleanup job and one that’s “bigger than Heartbleed.” (The latter is a reference to the critical security vulnerability in the OpenSSL cryptographic software library.)

These issues come on the heels of other security breaches and hacks, including the breach of the cloud-native database-as-a-service, TiDB Cloud, which thecompany announcedon Monday. Otherhackershave beenexploitingfour patched Plex Media Server flaws, collectively called Plex2Shell. And last week, cybersecurity companyBeyondTrust warned customersto patch a critical zero-day in its Remote Support product, which had been exploited since August.

Though the issues were unrelated to each other, their back-to-back arrival highlights the challenges cybersecurity teams now face. This is particularly important as AI could make it easier for attackers to exploit vulnerabilities once discovered.

articles.title: Year-old AI lab Flapping Airplanes raises $1B at a $6B valuation
articles.author: Julie Bort
articles.content:
Year-old startup Flapping Airplanes has wowed Silicon Valley with an impressive founding team and a mission to find ways to train large models with less data. On Wednesday, the companyannouncedit had raised a $1 billion Series A round, co-led by Index and Lux,reportedlyat a $6 billion valuation.

The round comes just nine months after the companylaunched with a $180 million seed roundfrom GV, Sequoia, and Index. That seed round had valued the company at $1.5 billion, so its valuation just quadrupled.

Other participants in the new round included earlier backers Sequoia, GV, and Kleiner Perkins. Valor, Atreides, Kleiner Perkins, A*, and Nvidia are also investors in the company.

Flapping Airplanes was founded by Aidan Smith and brothers Asher and Ben Spector. Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at the brain implant company Neuralink during college. Asher Spector was a statistics PhD at Stanford, while Ben Spector was a computer science PhD student at Stanford and founded Prod while at MIT.

Prod is an almost secret-society, five-year-oldstudent-run startup acceleratorthat has “become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley,” wroteSequoia partner David Cahn, a Flapping Planes investor, in a post earlier this year explaining why he invested. Together, the founders “are building the ‘young person’s AGI lab,’” as Cahn described it.

The founders describe their work as “the world’s most complete megakernel framework. It can perform entire training runs, serve inference, play video games, and even do all three simultaneously in a single kernel.” (A kernel is a program that runs on a GPU, and a megakernel bundles many tasks into one program.)

The founders claim the framework “can overlap memory-bound inference with compute-bound training,” meaning it can run a task that spends most of its time waiting for data to be fetched alongside one that spends most of its time doing math, so the chip is rarely sitting idle. The premise is that AI has barely scratched the surface of what GPUs can do, and they believe it can create intelligent systems “without ingesting half the internet.”

The goal is systems that cost less to train and run. “A model that’s a million times more data efficient is probably a million times easier to put into the economy,”Asher Spector told TechCrunchshortly after the startup launched.

They now have a fresh $1 billion to hire and attempt to turn that goal into reality.

articles.title: Automattic begins layoffs following board upheaval and executive departures
articles.author: Sarah Perez
articles.content:
Automattic, the parent company toWordPress.com, WooCommerce, Tumblr, and others, has begun layoffs, and insiders tell us they are bracing for more cuts to come.

Over at least the past week, the cuts have impacted its communications team, social team, WordPress.com, and its VIP enterprise business.

The departures represent more turmoil at Automattic, whose team is still reeling from the board’s failed attempt to oust CEO Matt Mullenweg in September, resulting in acomplete board turnoverand other exec departures, including its CFO,interim CFO, and chief legal officer.

Automattic’s director of communications, Megan Fox,posted about her departurelast week on LinkedIn, saying the move was an “unexpected end” and that her role had been “eliminated.”

Meanwhile, after TechCrunch reported that Automattic’s interim CFOJeremy Klaperman left earlier this month, only weeks after the board shake-up, Mullenwegposted on Xsuggesting Klaperman may have been “offended” by the company’s decision to seek external candidates to fill the role. (Internally, however, Mullenweg had asked Klaperman to reconsider leaving, we had heard.)

At one point, Mullenweg also shared personal information about one of the recently departed execs in the company’s internal Slack, according to screenshots viewed by TechCrunch. The post was related to a health matter impacting the person’s spouse and claimed that the company was not providing this person with much-needed COBRA insurance. Mullenweg said the exec was threatening to sue over this. Mullenweg also shared that his own fiancée had been impacted by the same health condition. Some employees told us they were shocked that the CEO would share something so private and personal in such a forum.

Throughout this month, TechCrunch has heard from different sources that members of Automattic’s team have also been let go, including those in marketing and product at WordPress.com.

Reached for comment about the layoffs last week, Mullenweg said the terminations were not above its normal numbers. Asked on Wednesday about the growing total, Mullenweg said that today he was “mostly focused on PHP.” (Heposted on Xabout thePHP security issuehitting the internet, which is taking priority.)

The company’s About page lists the total number of staff at 1,397, but insiders tell us that the plan is likely to spread out the layoffs over the months ahead, in the hopes of improving Automattic’s Q4 revenue figures ahead of a debt renegotiation that’s coming up in June.

In a statement shared with TechCrunch, Automattic spokesperson Chenda Ngak said, “We’re staggering our organizational changes to be more generous with severance and allow more time with each Automattician.”

Updated after publication with Automattic’s statement.

articles.title: Nirva raises $33M for a pendant that only listens to you
articles.author: Ivan Mehta
articles.content:
Ambient AI is having a moment. Amazonlaunched a new wrist-worn devicewith Bee; a former Plaud execlaunched ambient appsthrough a startup called Ambi, which aims to also build its own hardware; and Applelaunched Voice Intelligence featuresduring its iPhone launch in September. Now, a company calledNirvais betting on a jewelry-like pendant and its ability to listen only to the wearer.

The startup today announced a new $25 million pre-Series A round, adding to the $8 million it raised earlier in the year from investors like Lightspeed and South Park Commons, bringing its total raise to $33 million.

Nirva was founded in 2025 by two former Meta Reality Labs employees, Wei Lyu and Jason Chen, along with Hanying Hu, who founded a fashion and jewelry brand.

The company’s first device is a pendant, which can also be worn as a bracelet. The device weighs only around eight grams, making it easy to wear all day. Its battery lasts up to three days on a single charge.

Longer term, Nirva aims to release more devices.

In a call with TechCrunch, Nirva CEO Lyu said that the company wanted to build a wearable that blends in with fashion, but also provides value to users.

“This is a piece of jewelry that only focuses on listening to your own speech. We are not like a voice recorder or like a meeting note taker. One key difference between us, Taya, Vocci, or Sandbar Ring is that we’re always passively listening to your own speech. So it’s always on. It keeps modeling the user and modeling your mind,” Lyu said.

For ambient devices, privacy is a big question, as people might not like to be recorded all the time. Plus, devices like the Ray-Ban Meta have instilled fear in those who are around the person wearing the smart glasses that they are being recorded too.

Nirva gets around this problem by asking users to record snippets of their voice during onboarding and building its model based on that. During use, the device filters out conversations or data captured from the other people around the device. That means it’s only recording the wearer.

In addition, Nirva by default doesn’t keep any audio data or transcripts after processing the conversations.

Nirva is positioning itself as a personal insights company rather than a productivity startup. However, its app shows you reminders or action items and ways to act on them. Lyu said that through its app, the startup wants to help users show up for others in a better way in their lives.

“I think there’s no universal way to help everyone to solve their problems. We are building a tool to help people to improve their self-understanding, self-compassion, and self-awareness,” Lyu said.

The companion app parses users’ speech and creates insights that it infers are related to the user’s personality, including patterns, the people who tend to be around them, the places they’ve been to, and other daily notes. Lyu emphasized that the app shows users insights around their emotions, communication style, and ways they can improve.

Wyu gave an example of an incident when she forgot to thank her mother for something, and the app later nudged her with a reminder about this.

The company also said that, before it discards the audio, it’s able to track the tone, pitch, volume, and speed, which are useful for deriving emotion-related understandings that are then surfaced in the app.

Nirva will start taking orders for its devices in November, with an aim to ship them to early users by the end of the year. The $249 device will be available in silver, brushed silver, black, and gold.

The startup has competition in the AI wearables area. There are companies like former Apple employees’Taya, which is also building intelligent jewelry. Plus, startups like Friend and Bee are trying to be companion gadgets as well.

articles.title: DeepSeek reportedly raises $15B days after US restrictions
articles.author: Kate Park
articles.content:
Just two days afterthe U.S. orderedfederal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek’s AI technology from their systems over security concerns, the Chinese AI lab has raised about $15 billion, about 100 billion yuan, one of the biggest funding rounds in the country,Bloombergreported.

Potential investors include Chinese battery maker CATL and Tencent, the company behind WeChat, among others, according to the report.

The reported funding follows DeepSeek’s investment round in June, when it raised more than$7 billionat a valuation of $50 billion. The company was also reportedly seeking an additional $1.5 billion at a valuation of around $71 billionin July, with plans for a potential IPO in China as early as next year.

The Hangzhou-based AI startup is ramping up spending on AI infrastructure and open models for domestic and international markets, even as it faces restrictions in the U.S., the report said. Its expansion could further intensify competition among domestic rivals.

The massive funding round is the latest sign of investors pouring billions into AI companies around the world, including those in China, to compete in the global AI race.  Chinese company Kimi developerMoonshot AIsecured $2 billion at a $20 billion valuation in May.Manus AIraised more than $500 million earlier this month. Meanwhile, Chinese companies Zhipu AI (Z.ai) and MiniMax, which both went public in Hong Kong in January, have market capitalizations of roughly$29 billionand$7.2 billion, respectively, as of today.

DeepSeek was founded in 2023 byLiang Wenfeng, who previously co-founded Chinese quantitative hedge fund High-Flyer, which helped finance DeepSeek’s early development. The AI startup gained global attention in early 2025 with its free-to-use, open-weight RI reasoning model, challenging the dominance of US AI companies.  Liang still retains an estimated 81.6% stake in its Chinese operating entity following its earlier funding round, according to corporate ownership dataanalyzed by WireScreen.

DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a TechCrunch request for comment.
